Anaesthesia

Infiltration between the popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee (IPACK) vs. selective tibial nerve block for analgesia after total knee arthroplasty: a triple-blinded randomised controlled trial

Szyszko M, Wegrzyn J, Rossel JB et al. · 2026 Oct 18
Study Type: Triple-blinded, single-centre-style randomised controlled trial (n=90; centre number not stated in abstract)
Key Question: Does IPACK provide superior analgesia to selective tibial nerve block after total knee arthroplasty under spinal anaesthesia with a femoral triangle block?
Key Findings:
  • Day 1 cumulative IV morphine (primary outcome) did not differ: IPACK 6 (SD 7) mg vs tibial block 5 (SD 6) mg; p = 0.36. The superiority hypothesis was not supported.
  • No differences in pain scores at rest or on movement (days 1-3) or in functional outcomes (quadriceps strength, walking distance, range of motion).
  • Common peroneal nerve motor block occurred in 4/45 (9%) of the selective tibial group.
Clinical Relevance: Either technique is a reasonable posterior knee analgesic option within a multimodal TKA pathway, so choice can be guided by operator familiarity, block time and peroneal motor block risk.
Limitations: Opioid consumption was very low in both arms, so the trial may be unable to discriminate between techniques; the abstract reports no sample size justification or non-inferiority/equivalence margin.

Anaesthesia

Canadian evidence-based guidelines on spinal procedures for chronic pain

Bhatia A, Peng P, Shanthanna H et al. · 2026 Oct 18
Study Type: Clinical practice guideline (evidence-based, consensus panel; qualitative evidence synthesis).
Key Question: What are the indications, frequency, technical conduct, image-guidance requirements and complication management for common diagnostic and therapeutic spinal interventions in chronic spinal pain?
Key Findings:
  • The panel produced 15 key recommendations plus good clinical practice statements covering cervical, lumbar and sacroiliac joint procedures.
  • Recommendations were graded A to D, or I (insufficient), using USPSTF criteria, with certainty rated high, medium or low; consensus required at least 75% panel agreement.
  • The abstract does not report the specific recommendations, grades or procedure-level effect sizes.
Clinical Relevance: Provides a structured benchmark for UK pain services to compare against current practice, though it is a Canadian guideline and UK services follow NICE and local commissioning policy.
Limitations: Evidence was synthesised qualitatively rather than by formal meta-analysis, and the abstract gives no detail on search methods or the strength of individual recommendations, so the full text is needed before applying them.

Anaesthesia

Delivery and adherence of biomarker-guided antibiotic treatment protocols in the ADAPT-Sepsis clinical trial: an in-trial descriptive process evaluation of daily procalcitonin- and C-reactive protein-guided protocols

Lall R, Hossain A, Poole R et al. · 2026 Oct 20
Study Type: Pre-planned, embedded descriptive process evaluation within the multicentre ADAPT-Sepsis RCT (2760 adults, 41 UK critical care units).
Key Question: How well were procalcitonin- and CRP-guided antibiotic discontinuation protocols delivered, and how closely did clinicians adhere to the advice?
Key Findings:
  • PCT guidance produced "strong stop" advice 1.7 days earlier than CRP (95%CI -2.5 to -0.9); CRP guidance generated more standard care advice (-9.1%, 95%CI -10.9 to -7.3).
  • Overall adherence was higher with CRP than PCT (-6.8%, 95%CI -9.0 to -4.5), driven by more standard care advice and higher adherence to its later stop advice (-14.3%, 95%CI -21.8 to -6.8).
  • Non-adherence reasons were similar between arms: fixed-duration microbiology guidance, illness severity, persistent fever, and raised routine inflammatory markers.
Clinical Relevance: For UK intensivists, PCT may offer greater stewardship potential through earlier stopping, but this depends on clinicians accepting shorter courses than usual practice.
Limitations: This is a descriptive evaluation of process, not outcomes, so it cannot show whether earlier stopping or higher adherence affects patient safety or antibiotic exposure.

Anaesthesia

Optimum timing of cerebral computed tomography angiography for determination of death using neurological criteria: a retrospective sensitivity cohort study

Bohatyrewicz R, Sawicki M, Chamier-Ciemińska K et al. · 2026 Oct 21
Study Type: Retrospective single-population cohort study (n=118 ICU patients).
Key Question: Does the time elapsed from onset of brainstem areflexia signs affect the sensitivity of cerebral CTA for confirming cerebral circulatory arrest in determination of death using neurological criteria?
Key Findings:
  • Overall sensitivity was 87.3% (95% CI 79.6-92.5%); CTA failed to confirm circulatory arrest in 15/118 (13%).
  • 93.3% of false negatives occurred within 12 h of onset of brainstem areflexia.
  • Sensitivity was 67.4% (95% CI 51.3-80.5%) when performed ≤12 h versus 98.7% (95% CI 91.8-100%) when performed >12 h (p<0.001).
Clinical Relevance: Early CTA may under-detect cerebral circulatory arrest, so teams considering ancillary imaging in UK brainstem death testing should be aware that timing affects reliability, and a negative early scan does not exclude circulatory arrest.
Limitations: The retrospective design and the post hoc 12 h threshold (derived from the data, not prespecified) limit confidence, and the study evaluates sensitivity only, with no reference standard stated in the abstract.

Anaesthesia

Pain management after total shoulder arthroplasty: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management (PROSPECT) recommendations

Mrazek I, Desai N, Sauter AR et al. · 2026 Oct 22
Study Type: Systematic review with procedure-specific (PROSPECT) consensus recommendations; 30 RCTs and 7 systematic reviews/meta-analyses included from 1809 screened.
Key Question: What is the optimal multimodal analgesic regimen for adults undergoing total shoulder arthroplasty?
Key Findings:
  • Evidence supported paracetamol, NSAIDs, IV dexamethasone (8-10 mg), and interscalene block (local infiltration analgesia as an alternative) for improved postoperative analgesia.
  • Evidence was conflicting for continuous interscalene catheters and for liposomal bupivacaine (in block or infiltration); no evidence favoured any specific surgical technique.
  • Recommended regimen: paracetamol, peri- and postoperative NSAID, dexamethasone, single-shot interscalene block with bupivacaine or ropivacaine (not liposomal), and opioids for rescue only.
Clinical Relevance: Provides an evidence-graded template for shoulder arthroplasty analgesia that can inform UK enhanced recovery pathways and local protocol development, including a fallback where block expertise is unavailable.
Limitations: The abstract gives no effect sizes or certainty-of-evidence grading, and the recommendations rest on RCTs of variable quality and heterogeneous comparators.

Anaesthesia

Liberal vs. conventional pre-operative clear fluid fasting policies in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised and non-randomised studies

Nagase T, Takahashi K, Takagi T et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised and non-randomised studies (33 studies, 580,197 children).
Key Question: Does the incidence of pulmonary aspiration differ between liberal (<2 h) and conventional (≥2 h) pre-operative clear fluid fasting in children undergoing general anaesthesia or sedation?
Key Findings:
  • Pooled aspiration incidence was identical at 0.03% (95%CI 0.01–0.09%) under both policies; pooled RR from 14 studies was 0.77 (95%CI 0.40–1.47).
  • Vomiting without aspiration was similar: 0.76% (liberal) vs 0.99% (conventional), with overlapping wide confidence intervals.
  • Certainty of evidence was very low for both outcomes.
Clinical Relevance: Supports the safety of shortened clear fluid fasting in paediatric lists, which may reduce fasting-related distress and dehydration, though it does not by itself justify departing from current UK guidance (1 h clear fluids is already endorsed by APAGBI/ESAIC-aligned policies).
Limitations: Aspiration is extremely rare and the evidence is very low certainty, so the wide confidence interval around the RR cannot exclude a clinically meaningful difference.

Anesthesiology

Operating Room Air Filtration-Sterilization and Surgical Infections: The ORACLE Randomized Trial in 110,538 Surgeries

Sessler DI, Mascha EJ, Ekrami E et al. · 2026 Oct 19
Study Type: Cluster-randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (operating rooms randomised in 4-week blocks)
Key Question: Does supplemental operating room air purification reduce surgical wound infection, infection-related complications, or death within 30 days of surgery?
Key Findings:
  • Primary composite (inpatients, n=58,938): 8.1% active vs 8.2% sham; OR 0.98 (95% CI 0.92–1.05), P=0.609.
  • Secondary composite (inpatients and outpatients, n=107,334 analysed): 5.5% vs 5.6%; OR 0.98 (95% CI 0.93–1.05), P=0.669.
  • Stopped early for futility at the third interim analysis; no variation in effect over time.
Clinical Relevance: Supports not investing in supplemental air-purification units for SSI prevention and prioritising measures targeting direct wound contamination (e.g. NICE-aligned SSI bundles).
Limitations: Only one purification technology was tested (industry-funded, though the funder was not involved in data acquisition, analysis or manuscript preparation), so the findings may not generalise to other filtration systems or theatre ventilation designs.

Anesthesiology

Childhood Exposure to General Anesthesia For Surgery: Identification of a Subtle Post-Operative Cognitive Phenotype

Salaün JP, Menu I, Aguiar T et al. · 2026 Oct 21
Study Type: Ambidirectional cohort study (n=77, aged 9-11 years) with exploratory latent profile analysis.
Key Question: Is childhood general anaesthesia (GA) exposure for surgery associated with differences in executive function or visuo-spatial attention?
Key Findings:
  • No difference in overall executive function between GA-exposed (mean age at exposure 4.5 ± 3.0 years) and unexposed children (χ²(1)=0.01, p=0.92).
  • Exploratory latent profile analysis identified "Efficient" and "Vulnerable" executive control profiles. GA exposure was associated with lower odds of Efficient profile membership (OR 0.71; reported 95% CI 0.705-0.710).
  • GA-exposed children showed higher global-local precedence (estimate 0.53, 95% CI 0.04-1.01, p=0.036).
Clinical Relevance: Supports reassurance that a single early GA exposure is not linked to broad executive deficits, though subtle phenotypic differences remain hypothesis-generating for paediatric anaesthesia counselling in the UK.
Limitations: Small sample with exploratory profile analysis (the implausibly narrow CI suggests possible model instability), and the ambidirectional design with no stated adjustment for surgical indication or confounders limits causal inference.
